```{r setup, include=FALSE}
ready <- requireNamespace("gtsummary", quietly = TRUE) &&
  utils::packageVersion("gtsummary") >= "2.6.1" &&
  requireNamespace("gt", quietly = TRUE) &&
  requireNamespace("rmarkdown", quietly = TRUE) &&
  rmarkdown::pandoc_available()
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = ready)
```

`cifreport()` writes a self-contained HTML report and invisibly returns the
underlying tables, plots, fitted objects, and analysis log. Install
gtsummary (at least 2.6.1), gt, knitr, and rmarkdown, and make Pandoc
available to rmarkdown before running the example.

## Two outcomes in one report

In the diabetes cohort, code 1 identifies diabetic retinopathy, code 2
identifies a macrovascular complication, and code 0 identifies censoring.
For the survival endpoint, either complication is an event. Both outcomes
use the same follow-up column in this example. An endpoint measured from
a different origin can name its own follow-up column.

```{r report}
library(cifmodeling)
data(diabetes.complications)
cohort <- transform(diabetes.complications, all_event = epsilon != 0)

report <- cifreport(
  cohort,
  exposure = c("Fruit intake" = "fruitq1"),
  code.exposure.ref = 0,
  characteristics = c("age", "sex"),
  outcomes = list(
    Retinopathy = list(time = "t", event = "epsilon", time.point = c(4, 8)),
    "Complication-free survival" = list(
      time = "t", event = "all_event", outcome.type = "survival", time.point = c(3, 8)
    )
  ),
  overall = TRUE,
  output.file = tempfile(fileext = ".html")
)

report$tables$All[["Fruit intake"]]$table3
```

Omit `output.file` to write `yyyymmdd_cohort_analysis_report.html` in the
current directory. Set `data.name = "diabetes.complications"` to use the
original dataset name in the filename and the default report title.
Use `subset.condition = "age >= 50"` to restrict the analysis population.
Use `subgroup = "sex"` to report the selected population as a whole and each
observed level of `sex` within it. Use `exposure = c("Fruit intake" = "fruitq1", Sex = "sex")`
to add a grouping. Each population/exposure combination gets one section.
Factor levels determine group order. The first observed level is the default
risk-ratio reference. Use a named vector or list such as
`code.exposure.ref = list("Fruit intake" = 0)` to select references by exposure.

Use `level.strata = c(0, 1)`, `label.strata = c("Other intake", "Low intake")`,
and `order.strata = c(1, 0)` to display the low-intake group first in the
tables and curves. The reference is specified with its original code.
For multiple exposures, supply a named list for each strata argument,
such as `label.strata = list("Fruit intake" = c("0" = "Other intake", "1" = "Low intake"))`.
Subgroups use the same labels for their observed exposure levels.

## Reading each section

1. **Patient characteristics.** A gtsummary table describes the subjects
   in each group. Missing baseline values appear in separate rows by
   default. Use `table1.args = list(label = list(age ~ "Age (years)"))`
   to change a label, or `overall = TRUE` to include the whole population.
   Characteristics with value labels (a named `labels` attribute) are
   summarized as categorical. Exposure value labels also appear in the table
   titles and are used as group labels unless overridden by `label.strata`.
   The p-value column compares the exposure groups using the default
   tests in `gtsummary::add_p()`. A characteristic needs at least two
   observed values and nonmissing data in at least two exposure groups to
   be tested.
   The text below the table gives group sizes and identifies characteristics
   with p-values below 0.05.
2. **Observed events over all follow-up.** The table names the time and event
   columns and shows primary, competing, and censoring counts alongside their codes.
   The text below it flags outcomes with fewer than five primary events in
   at least one exposure group.
3. **Cumulative counts and estimated probabilities.** Counts use
   `observed_time <= time.point` and include events tied at the requested
   time. Kaplan-Meier survival (KM) or primary-event Aalen-Johansen cumulative
   incidence (AJ) and pointwise confidence intervals use the same right-continuous
   convention. Enter times in the units of the follow-up column. Observed
   counts remain available beyond follow-up, where estimates and intervals
   are omitted for the affected groups. An outcome's `estimator` can request
   `"1-KM"` for event probability or `"1-AJ"` for the complement of the CIF.
   The text below the table gives the observed follow-up range across groups
   in the current analysis population and identifies nonpositive observed times.
4. **Crude risk ratios.** Each horizon has a separate intercept-only
   `polyreg()` nuisance model. For survival, the risk is one minus survival
   at the horizon. For competing risks, both cause-specific cumulative
   incidence ratios are reported from the joint fit. These are unadjusted
   associations. A requested horizon must be within the observed follow-up
   of every group, and a competing-risk fit requires both causes by that time.
5. **Curve comparison tests.** The log-rank test compares survival curves
   and Gray's test compares primary-event cumulative incidence curves over
   follow-up. Each outcome has one test per section.

**Figure 1** contains one plot per outcome using the fitted curves from
Table 3. The plots show the outcome scale, group labels and risk tables.

## Supported data and analysis status

The report supports unweighted right-censored follow-up with one row per
subject, distinct non-negative integer codes, and one competing code per
competing-risk outcome. Logical events and numeric codes stored as factor
levels or character strings are supported. Supported comparisons include
binary and multi-level groups. Left truncation, time-dependent covariates,
recurrent events, adjustment, and simultaneous confidence bands are
outside the reporting interface.

Rows where a subset condition evaluates to `NA` are excluded. Within each
subset, missing group values skip the section. Missing follow-up
times or event values skip the affected outcome. An empty population
produces a status entry. With a single observed group, the report keeps
the descriptive tables and plot. An absent reference level affects risk
ratios only. The status log records these cases as well as unsupported
horizons, warnings and estimation failures. A failure in one fit leaves
unrelated results available.

Subjects with missing subgroup values contribute to the overall analysis.
For a subgroup level with zero observed events for an outcome, the report
includes the counts in Table 2 and skips Tables 3–5 and Figure 1 for that
outcome. In a competing-risk outcome, either a primary event or a competing
event counts toward this check.
